passage:
"Why is she moving her hands like that?" asked Wasim, a family friend visiting for tea.
"Rekha's deaf," said her mother. "We sign with her at home. That's her sign for milk."
"She's already talking? She's so small."
"In signs, yes. Watch." Her mother signed back and fetched the cup.
Rekha drank, then made another sign and pushed the cup away.
"And that one means 'all done'," her mother said.

qa.q: What did Rekha's first sign ask for?
qa.a: Milk.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling when she pushed the cup away?
qa.a: She was likely satisfied and content, and used her sign to say she was finished.

qa.q: What could Wasim do to communicate with Rekha?
qa.a: Ask the family to show him a few of Rekha's signs and use them with her.

qa.q: How does Wasim see Rekha's signing at first?
qa.a: Wasim is surprised and curious, not expecting such a small child to be "talking" already.

grounding: A deaf toddler uses her family's signs for "milk" and "all done", showing she communicates well before speech.

passage: Daycare note, Wednesday. At snack time Saurabh made the sign his family uses for "more" and looked straight at me. I said "More?" and made the same sign, and gave him more apple. When he had finished, he made his "all done" sign and pushed his plate away. His parents showed us these signs last week. I say the word each time I sign, and he seems pleased to be understood. Hansa, daycare teacher

qa.q: What did Saurabh get more of?
qa.a: More apple.

qa.q: What did Saurabh seem to feel when Hansa understood his sign?
qa.a: He seemed pleased and satisfied to be understood.

qa.q: What habit of Hansa's supports Saurabh's language?
qa.a: Hansa uses the family's signs and says the word each time, linking signs and speech.

qa.q: How might Saurabh's parents feel reading the note?
qa.a: They would likely feel glad that daycare is using the signs they shared.

grounding: A teacher uses a toddler's family signs for "more" and "all done" before he speaks, helping him feel understood.

passage:
In the small-town kitchen, Karthik, Salma's older cousin, was feeding her rice. After a few spoons, Salma shook both hands in the air, fast.
"More?" Karthik held out another spoon. Salma turned her head and shook her hands again, harder.
"That's her 'all done'," her mother called from the stove. "We taught her with the hands."
"Oh! All done," Karthik said, putting the spoon down. Salma stopped shaking her hands and smiled.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeding Salma?
qa.a: Rice.

qa.q: What was Salma feeling when she shook her hands harder?
qa.a: She was frustrated at not being understood, as she wanted to say she was finished; she smiled when Karthik understood.

qa.q: What could Karthik do next time he helps with meals?
qa.a: Ask the family about Salma's gestures so he can read them from the start.

qa.q: How does Karthik react when he understands?
qa.a: He seems surprised and glad to learn her sign, putting the spoon down at once.

grounding: A toddler uses a family gesture for "all done", and her cousin learns to read it.

passage:
On the floor of their Nairobi flat, Wanjiru held a spoon to her doll's mouth. "Baby hungry. Waaa!" she wailed for the doll, then fed it. "Mmm. Good baby."
Mateo, a family friend, looked up. "Are you hungry, Wanjiru?"
She looked at him as if he were silly. "No. Baby hungry."
She tucked the doll under a cloth and patted it. "Sleep, baby."

qa.q: What did Wanjiru do after feeding the doll?
qa.a: She tucked the doll under a cloth and patted it.

qa.q: What was Wanjiru feeling as she fed and tucked in her doll?
qa.a: She seemed happy and absorbed in caring for the doll, practising the role of a carer.

qa.q: What would you advise Mateo about reading her play?
qa.a: Treat the doll's words as pretend, a way she practises roles, not as a report of her own needs.

qa.q: How does Mateo first read the doll's "hunger"?
qa.a: He wonders if Wanjiru herself is hungry, taking the play too literally.

grounding: A toddler plays at feeding a doll, and an adult learns to read the doll's needs as pretend, not a literal report.

passage: I'm Darshan, Salma's cousin. On Sunday she made her teddy talk in a squeaky voice. "Teddy scared. Doctor! No!" Teddy shook and hid under the pillow. I thought Salma was scared, so I asked her. She shrugged and made teddy come out. "Teddy brave now." Her mother said she has a check-up this week. Maybe Salma was practising. Maybe it was just a game.

qa.q: Where did the teddy hide?
qa.a: Under the pillow.

qa.q: What might Salma have been feeling as she made the teddy talk?
qa.a: She may have felt a little worried about her check-up and was trying the feeling out safely through teddy; making teddy "brave" suggests she felt more confident by the end.

qa.q: What could Salma's family do with this play?
qa.a: Join in gently, perhaps giving teddy a pretend check-up, without treating it as a literal report.

qa.q: How does Darshan read teddy's fear?
qa.a: Darshan wonders if Salma is scared herself, then isn't sure if it was practice or just a game.

grounding: A cousin watches a toddler make her teddy talk about fear, and learns to read it as practice and play.

passage:
Monday: Hemant slipped a sock puppet on his hand and roared at Pema, his mother. "Rrrah!" She pretended to hide.
Thursday: the puppet "cried". Hemant patted its head. "Shh, puppy."
The next Monday, at dinner, the puppet said in a squeaky voice, "Hemant eat all dinner!" Hemant's plate was still full. Pema laughed. "The puppet says so, does it?"

qa.q: What did the puppet say at dinner?
qa.a: "Hemant eat all dinner!"

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling when he patted the crying puppet?
qa.a: He seemed caring and gentle, trying out the feeling of comforting someone.

qa.q: What did Pema's laugh at dinner show she understood?
qa.a: That the puppet's words were play, not a true report, since his plate was still full.

qa.q: How might Pema feel as Hemant's puppet play grows?
qa.a: She likely feels amused and fond, enjoying his growing imagination. 😊

grounding: Over a week a toddler uses a sock puppet to roar, comfort and "report", which his mother reads as play.

passage:
Music boomed from the society courtyard in Mumbai. Jagdish bounced on his toes, clapping and shouting "Ya-ya-ya!", a scrap of the song, beaming at his brother Pankaj.
Late that night, the music was still playing softly. Jagdish sat on Pankaj's lap, thumb in mouth, swaying slowly from side to side, eyes half closed.
"Same song," Pankaj told his mother. "Different dance."

qa.q: What did Jagdish shout while bouncing?
qa.a: "Ya-ya-ya!"

qa.q: What did Jagdish's swaying late at night show?
qa.a: He was tired and calming himself toward sleep, while his earlier bouncing showed joy and excitement.

qa.q: How could the family use the difference in his movements?
qa.a: Join the bouncing when he's excited, and help him rest when the slow swaying starts.

qa.q: How does Pankaj see the two ways Jagdish moved?
qa.a: Pankaj notices that the same song brought out joy earlier and sleepy soothing later.

grounding: A toddler bounces and claps to music with joy and later sways slowly to soothe himself when tired.

passage:
"Listen, Simran, she's singing."
"Tinkle, tinkle!" Devika bounced on the bed, clapping.
"She wants you to join in," said Devika's mother.
Simran sang the rest, and Devika bounced harder.
An hour later, after her bath: "Why is she swaying so slowly now?"
Devika was rocking side to side, humming, rubbing her eye.
"That's her sleepy song," said her mother.

qa.q: What was Devika singing?
qa.a: "Tinkle, tinkle!"

qa.q: What was Devika feeling as she swayed slowly after her bath?
qa.a: She was tired and soothing herself toward sleep, not playing.

qa.q: What could Simran do during the slow swaying?
qa.a: Sing softly or stay quiet and help Devika get ready for sleep, instead of starting a lively song.

qa.q: How does Devika's mother read the two moments?
qa.a: She knows the bouncing means Devika wants to join in, and the slow swaying means she's sleepy.

grounding: An aunt learns that a toddler's bouncing song means joy and a wish to join in, while slow swaying means tiredness.

passage: Daycare note, Friday. At music time Santosh bounced and clapped all the way through "the wheels on the bus", singing "round and round" at the right moments. At nap time he sat on his mat swaying side to side, humming the same tune very softly, until he lay down and slept. Same song, two moods: joining in, then settling himself. Chinmay, daycare teacher

qa.q: Which song did Santosh sing at music time?
qa.a: "The wheels on the bus".

qa.q: What was Santosh feeling when he swayed and hummed at nap time?
qa.a: He was tired and was soothing himself toward sleep, unlike the excited joining in at music time.

qa.q: What would you advise staff about Santosh's swaying?
qa.a: Read it by context: at nap time it means he's settling, so keep things quiet around him.

qa.q: How might Santosh's parents feel reading this note?
qa.a: They would likely be pleased to learn how he enjoys music and uses it to calm down.

grounding: A teacher notes a toddler's singing and bouncing at music time and soothing swaying at nap time.

passage:
Rajni pressed a red crayon so hard it snapped, and went on scribbling with both pieces.
"What is it?" asked her grandfather. "A flower? A house?"
"Don't ask what it is, Papa," said Leela, her mother. "Try, 'You pressed so hard! Lots of red!'"
He tried it. Rajni grinned up at him, grabbed a blue crayon and scribbled even faster, humming.

qa.q: What happened to the red crayon?
qa.a: It snapped because Rajni pressed so hard.

qa.q: What was Rajni feeling as she scribbled faster and hummed?
qa.a: She was joyful and absorbed in the feeling of making marks, and pleased to be noticed.

qa.q: Why did Leela suggest a different comment?
qa.a: Because Rajni's marks are about exploring, not pictures, so praising her effort and colour fits better than asking what it is.

qa.q: How might the grandfather feel when Rajni grins at him?
qa.a: He probably feels pleased and closer to her, seeing that the new comment worked.

grounding: A mother suggests praising a toddler's effort in scribbling rather than asking what it is, as the marks are exploration.

passage: Daycare note, Tuesday. Bhavna put both hands in the yellow paint and smeared them across the paper, then her arms, then the table, squealing. I did not ask what she was painting. I said, "Big, swirly marks! Your hands are all yellow!" She pressed her palms down again and again, watching the prints. She was very happy. Please send old clothes on paint days. Jeevan, daycare teacher

qa.q: What colour was the paint?
qa.a: Yellow.

qa.q: What was Bhavna feeling as she smeared the paint?
qa.a: She was joyful and delighted with the feel of the paint and the marks her hands made.

qa.q: Why did Jeevan describe the marks instead of asking what she was painting?
qa.a: Because her painting is about exploring and sensory joy, not making a picture of something.

qa.q: How might Bhavna's parents feel reading this note?
qa.a: They may smile at her happy mess, and be glad of the reminder about old clothes.

grounding: A teacher describes a toddler's paint smears instead of asking what they are, valuing sensory exploration.

passage:
By the village river, Jomon sat in the wet mud, squashing it between his fingers and slapping it flat.
Chetan, the older boy from next door, crouched beside him. "What are you making, Jomon? A pot?"
Jomon just squished another handful and laughed.
Chetan grinned and pushed his own hands into the mud. "You like the squishy feel!" Jomon slapped the mud again, delighted.

qa.q: Where was Jomon playing?
qa.a: In the wet mud by the village river.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling as he squashed the mud?
qa.a: He was delighted by the squishy feel, enjoying the sensation rather than making something.

qa.q: What did Chetan do well after his question?
qa.a: He switched from asking what it was to naming what Jomon enjoyed, and joined in.

qa.q: What would change if Chetan had kept asking what Jomon was making?
qa.a: Jomon couldn't answer, and the fun of simply exploring might have been interrupted.

grounding: An older boy learns that a toddler's mud-squashing is sensory joy, and names it instead of asking what it is.

passage: I'm Avni, Baljeet's big sister. Every morning Nani pulls his woolly cap on, and every morning Baljeet pulls it off, scratching his forehead, and screams. Nani says he's being stubborn. But I saw the red lines on his forehead. So on Tuesday I gave him my soft cotton cap. He touched it, pulled it on himself and kept it on all the way to the bus stop.

qa.q: What did Avni give Baljeet on Tuesday?
qa.a: Her soft cotton cap.

qa.q: What was Baljeet likely feeling when he pulled off the woolly cap?
qa.a: He was uncomfortable, probably itchy, and upset, which is why he scratched and screamed.

qa.q: What did Avni notice that Nani didn't?
qa.a: The red lines on Baljeet's forehead, a sign the wool was irritating him.

qa.q: How does Nani see Baljeet pulling off the cap?
qa.a: Nani thinks he is being stubborn, not uncomfortable.

grounding: A sister notices her toddler brother refuses a woolly cap because it itches, not out of defiance.

passage:
Monday: Santosh screamed when Tushar held up the blue T-shirt. He pointed at the orange one. "That!" Tushar gave in.
Wednesday: the orange T-shirt was in the wash. Santosh screamed again. Tushar held up two others. "Green or yellow?"
The next Monday: Tushar held up the orange and the green. Santosh thought, chose green, and pulled it on himself.

qa.q: Which T-shirt did Santosh choose the next Monday?
qa.a: The green one.

qa.q: What was Santosh feeling when he screamed on Wednesday?
qa.a: He was frustrated and upset that his favourite orange shirt was missing and he had no say.

qa.q: Which of Tushar's choices worked, and why?
qa.a: Offering two shirts to choose from worked, because Santosh got a small choice and calmed down.

qa.q: How might Tushar feel the next Monday?
qa.a: He would likely feel relieved and pleased that dressing was easy. 🙂

grounding: Over a week a father learns to offer his toddler clothing choices, supporting autonomy instead of fighting.

passage:
In the Delhi flat, Zainab, the nanny, buttoned Sarika into her new frock for the party. Sarika tugged at the neck, whining, and tried to pull it off.
"Such a pretty frock," said a visiting aunty. "Don't be naughty."
Zainab ran a finger inside the collar. Scratchy lace, and a pink mark on Sarika's neck. She changed her into the soft cotton one. Sarika stopped whining and twirled.

qa.q: What did Zainab find inside the collar?
qa.a: Scratchy lace, and a pink mark on Sarika's neck.

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling when she tugged at the neck and whined?
qa.a: She was uncomfortable and irritated by the scratchy lace, not being naughty.

qa.q: What did Zainab do that was wise?
qa.a: She checked the collar before deciding and changed Sarika into a soft frock.

qa.q: How does the visiting aunty see Sarika's tugging?
qa.a: The aunty sees it as naughtiness, not discomfort.

grounding: A nanny finds that a toddler's refusal of a frock is about scratchy lace, not defiance, and changes it.

passage:
At the colony birthday party in Bhopal, everyone clapped as the cake came out. Ankita, on her grandmother Usha's lap, looked around at all the clapping hands. Then she clapped too, a beat late, hands barely meeting.
When they sang the birthday song, Ankita waved both arms along with the older children, beaming. Usha waved hers too, and Ankita waved harder.

qa.q: What came out when everyone clapped?
qa.a: The cake.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling as she waved her arms with the song?
qa.a: She was delighted and felt part of the group, copying the older children.

qa.q: What did Usha do that encouraged Ankita?
qa.a: She waved along too, joining Ankita's imitation and sharing the fun.

qa.q: How might the older children see Ankita copying them?
qa.a: They might find it cute and feel pleased that she's joining in.

grounding: A toddler claps late and waves along with a group song, showing delight and belonging through imitation.

passage:
"Look, Dilnaz, she's waving her hands with the song!"
At the sangeet, the ladies were clapping and swaying in a circle. Elizabeth, on the edge of the rug, waved her hands up and down, clapped, and waved again.
"She's copying Aunty Farida," Dilnaz laughed.
"She wants to be in the circle."
"Then let's go." Dilnaz carried Elizabeth into the circle, and Elizabeth clapped with all her might.

qa.q: Where did Dilnaz carry Elizabeth?
qa.a: Into the circle.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth feeling as she waved and clapped on the edge of the rug?
qa.a: She was delighted by the music and eager to join the group, copying the adults.

qa.q: Which of Dilnaz's choices worked, and why?
qa.a: Carrying her into the circle worked, because it let Elizabeth really belong and join in.

qa.q: How might the ladies in the circle feel when Elizabeth joins?
qa.a: They would probably be pleased and amused to have the littlest one clapping with them.

passage: Daycare note, Monday. During the goodbye song, Uday sat in the circle watching the others wave. By the second verse he was waving too, both hands, a little out of time. When everyone clapped at the end, he clapped as well and looked around at the others, grinning. He's starting to join in with the group. Yash, daycare teacher

qa.q: When did Uday start waving?
qa.a: By the second verse of the goodbye song.

qa.q: What was Uday feeling when he clapped and looked around, grinning?
qa.a: He was delighted and proud to be doing what the group was doing, feeling part of it.

qa.q: How could staff encourage Uday's joining in?
qa.a: Smile back and keep the songs familiar, so he can copy and join in more.

qa.q: How might Uday's parents feel reading this note?
qa.a: They would likely be pleased to hear he's joining in with the group.

grounding: A teacher notes a toddler beginning to wave and clap along with the group, learning shared signals through imitation.

passage:
In the colony lane in Mysuru, Harsha squatted beside the neighbour's sleepy dog and patted it gently, over and over. Then he toddled to his mother and planted a wet kiss on her knee.
His uncle Zubin knelt. "One for me too, Harsha?"
Harsha shook his head and hid behind his mother.
"Okay," Zubin said easily. "Maybe tomorrow." Harsha peeped out and waved.

qa.q: What did Harsha kiss?
qa.a: His mother's knee.

qa.q: What did Harsha seem to feel toward the dog and his mother?
qa.a: He seemed affectionate and gentle, patting the dog and kissing his mother.

qa.q: Which of Zubin's choices respected Harsha, and why?
qa.a: Accepting the "no" easily and saying "Maybe tomorrow" respected Harsha's right to choose whom he kisses.

qa.q: How might Zubin feel when Harsha says no?
qa.a: He might feel a little disappointed but takes it lightly, which helps Harsha stay relaxed.

grounding: A toddler shows affection to a dog and his mother, and his uncle respects his refusal of a kiss.

passage:
"Sahil, he's kissing your arm," said their mother.
Jeevan had climbed into his big brother's lap on the sofa and was pressing little kisses on Sahil's sleeve.
"Aww, Jeevu." Sahil squeezed him, then started tickling.
"No!" Jeevan squirmed. "No!"
Sahil stopped straight away. "Okay. No tickles."
Jeevan snuggled back into his lap and patted his cheek.

qa.q: Where was Jeevan sitting?
qa.a: In Sahil's lap on the sofa.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling as he kissed Sahil's arm?
qa.a: He felt affectionate and close to his big brother.

qa.q: Why was it right for Sahil to stop tickling?
qa.a: Because Jeevan said no, and stopping showed him his "no" about his body is respected.

qa.q: How might Sahil feel when Jeevan snuggles back in?
qa.a: He likely feels warm and glad, knowing Jeevan still trusts him. 🤍

grounding: A toddler shows affection to his brother and says no to tickling, and the brother respects it.

passage: Childminder's note, Thursday. Divyansh spent a long time with our old cat today, patting her very gently and kissing the top of her head. At pick-up, I opened my arms for a goodbye hug, and he turned away and ran to his Papa. I just waved instead. He waved back from Papa's shoulder. He's very loving, and he's learning he can choose. Eshaan, childminder

qa.a: He patted her very gently and kissed the top of her head.

qa.q: What might Divyansh have been feeling when he turned away from the hug?
qa.a: He probably wanted his Papa at that moment and felt ready to go, not unfriendly; his wave back shows he still felt warm toward Eshaan.

qa.q: What did Eshaan's choice to wave instead teach Divyansh?
qa.a: That he can say no to a hug and still stay friends.

qa.q: How might Divyansh's Papa feel reading this note?
qa.a: He would likely feel pleased that Divyansh is affectionate and that his choice was respected.

grounding: A childminder notes a toddler's gentle affection with a cat and respects his refusal of a goodbye hug.

passage:
In the village courtyard, Kashish, Sabina's older cousin, stuck out her tongue and bleated like a goat. "Mehhh!" Sabina giggled. Kashish did it again, crossing her eyes. Sabina laughed so hard she fell over.
Later, a visitor from the next village tried the same goat face. Sabina stared, went quiet and hid behind Kashish.

qa.q: What animal did Kashish imitate?
qa.a: A goat.

qa.q: Why did Sabina hide from the visitor making the same face?
qa.a: She felt unsure and a little worried with someone unfamiliar, so the face felt strange rather than funny.

qa.q: What could the visitor do to get a laugh later?
qa.a: Spend time around Sabina first so she feels safe, before trying silly faces.

qa.q: How might Kashish feel when Sabina hides behind her?
qa.a: Kashish probably feels trusted and protective of her little cousin.

grounding: A toddler finds her cousin's goat face hilarious but is worried by the same face from a stranger, showing amusement depends on trust.

passage:
At breakfast in their Lima flat, Wei balanced a sock on his head, wobbled, and pretended to sneeze it off. "Achoo!"
Rosa stared, then burst into giggles. "Again!"
He did it again. She laughed harder, drumming her spoon.
The third time, she grabbed the sock and put it on her own head. "Choo!" she shouted, and it fell into her porridge.

qa.q: Where did the sock land in the end?
qa.a: In Rosa's porridge.

qa.q: What was Rosa feeling when she put the sock on her own head?
qa.a: She was amused and playful, wanting to share in the silly game.

qa.q: What could Wei do to keep the fun going?
qa.a: Keep repeating the game and let Rosa take turns, since the familiar joke feels safe and funny to her.

qa.q: How might Wei feel when the sock falls into the porridge?
qa.a: He likely laughs, amused, maybe groaning at the mess. 😄

grounding: A toddler giggles at her father's silly sock game, feeling safe enough to join the joke.

passage: I'm Nitin. On the train home I sat across from a little boy called Joseph and his mother. I made a funny face at him, cheeks puffed, eyes crossed. His face crumpled and he turned into his mother's shoulder. I felt terrible. Then his mother made the very same face at him. Joseph peeked, and started to giggle. Same face. I think it was just that I was a stranger.

qa.q: What funny face did Nitin make?
qa.a: Nitin puffed cheeks and crossed eyes.

qa.q: What did Joseph feel when Nitin made the face, and when his mother did?
qa.a: With Nitin, a stranger, he felt worried and upset; with his mother, he felt safe and amused.

qa.q: What could Nitin do differently with a small child?
qa.a: Smile gently from a distance first, since silly faces from strangers can scare a toddler.

qa.q: How does Nitin feel after Joseph turns away?
qa.a: Nitin feels terrible, then understands it was about being a stranger.

grounding: A stranger's silly face worries a toddler while the same face from his mother makes him giggle, showing amusement depends on trust.

passage: Daycare note, Thursday. When I blew bubbles in the garden today, Madhav gasped, his mouth making a big "O", and clapped fast. The bubbles popped and his clapping stopped just as quickly. I blew more. Same gasp, same clap, every time. We did it maybe fifteen times, and he never got tired of it. Wasim, daycare teacher

qa.q: What did Madhav do when he saw the bubbles?
qa.a: He gasped, his mouth making a big "O", and clapped fast.

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling each time the bubbles appeared?
qa.a: He felt a burst of delighted surprise, which faded quickly and returned each time.

qa.q: Why was repeating the bubbles a good idea?
qa.a: Because repeating the surprise let Madhav enjoy the same safe delight again and again.

qa.q: How might Madhav's parents feel reading this note?
qa.a: They would probably smile and feel happy to picture his joy.

grounding: A teacher repeats bubbles for a toddler who gasps and claps in delighted surprise each time.

passage:

qa.a: A paper pinwheel.

qa.q: What was Shankar feeling when the pinwheel spun?
qa.a: He was delighted and surprised, gasping and clapping each time.

qa.a: She likely feels happy and pleased with her small purchase. 🎉

passage:

Yara gasped, hands flying up, and then clapped. "Again!"
Felix set it up again. Zoom. Gasp. Clap.

passage: I'm Rukmini, from the flat downstairs. On Wednesday the first rain of the season started, and Samir, on his balcony, let out a squeal I could hear from my kitchen. qa.a: The raindrops, with his arms stretched out.

qa.q: What might Samir have been feeling as he squealed and bounced?
qa.a: He was likely overjoyed and excited by the first rain.

qa.q: What did Samir's father do that helps Samir learn about his feelings?
qa.a: He shared the joy with a laugh and named it, "You're so happy!"

qa.q: How does Rukmini experience Samir's squeal?
qa.a: Rukmini hears it from the kitchen and seems cheered by his joy.

grounding: A neighbour sees a toddler squeal and bounce at the first rain, and his father names the joy.

passage:
Sunday: Tanuja squealed and bounced when the neighbour's puppy licked her hand. Kavitha beamed back. "Happy! You're so happy!"
Wednesday: on the swing, Tanuja squealed again, beaming. "Happy!" Kavitha said.
The next Sunday: Tanuja ran to Kavitha, pointing at the puppy, and shouted, "Happy!"

qa.q: What did the puppy do on Sunday?
qa.a: It licked Tanuja's hand.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling when she ran to Kavitha shouting "Happy!"?
qa.a: She was joyful and excited, and wanted to share that joy with her mother.

qa.q: What habit of Kavitha's helped Tanuja name her joy?
qa.a: She smiled back and named the feeling, "Happy!", each time Tanuja showed it.

qa.q: How might Kavitha feel the next Sunday?
qa.a: She would likely feel delighted and proud that Tanuja can now tell her the feeling.

grounding: Over a week a mother names her toddler's joy until the child uses the word to share it.

passage:
In their Chennai flat, Yamini opened the cage, and Thatha's green parrot hopped onto her finger. Jahnavi squealed so loudly the parrot flapped. She bounced on the spot, beaming, hands clasped.
Yamini beamed back. "You're so happy! Look, parrot on Amma's finger." Jahnavi squealed again, softer this time, and reached out one careful finger.

qa.q: Whose parrot was it?
qa.a: Thatha's green parrot.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling as she bounced and beamed?
qa.a: She was bursting with joy and excitement at seeing the parrot on her mother's finger.

qa.q: What did Yamini do that helps Jahnavi understand her joy?
qa.a: She shared the smile and named the feeling, "You're so happy!"

qa.q: How might the parrot experience Jahnavi's loud squeal?
qa.a: It was startled, flapping its wings, which may be why Jahnavi's next squeal was softer.

grounding: A toddler squeals and beams at a parrot, and her mother shares the joy and names it.
